newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman asks U.S. to delay deporting Nicaraguans.
newsitem.headline: Aleman asks U.S. to delay deporting Nicaraguans.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman said on Monday he would ask the U.S. government to give Nicaraguans who face deportation from the United States temporary legal immigration status.

Thousands of Nicaraguans in the United States face imminent deportation due to new immigration laws that came into effect on Jan. 1, and Nicaragua lacks the infrastructure and jobs to absorb them, Aleman said on his first working day in office after his Friday inauguration.
"I'm not going to ask President Bill Clinton to give permanent residence to these people, only that he give them a temporary immigration status," he said on state-owned television.

Aleman said he had already met U.S. ambassador to Nicaragua Lino Gutierrez to discuss the issue and would make the request official on his next visit to the United States. The date of the visit was not specified.
An estimated 200,000 Nicaraguans live in Miami alone, many of whom fled Nicaragua in the 1980s during the rule of the left-wing Sandinista government, which confiscated private property.

Aleman wants the exile community to invest in Nicaragua and for skilled professionals to return to help spark economic growth in Nicaragua, the second poorest country in Latin America, but he knows the country cannot absorb a mass return of unskilled labour looking for work, analysts said.

"Today it is certain that we cannot receive at one blow this 'invasion' of Nicaraguans if it comes as an avalanche. The housing infrastructure is precarious and the generation of employment at this moment is almost zero," Aleman said.
But Aleman repeated his offer that Nicaraguans living abroad who want to return home can bring their personal belongings and professional equipment and machinery back to Nicaragua tax-free.
"The professionals who fled Nicaragua in the 1980s and have not had the opportunity to return, Nicaragua needs them," he said.
Nicaragua has a population of 4.3 million people with 52 percent of its work force either unemployed or underemployed, according to Ministry of the Economy statistics.
